background.definition: Orchitis is an acute inflammatory reaction of the testicles secondary to an infection. Pyogenic orchitis usually results from an inflammatory process in the epididymis.

list.listitem: There are approximately 600,000 cases of epididymitis per year in the United States.
Orchitis was seen in 58% of men diagnosed with epididymitis in one study that reviewed the clinical presentation of epididymitis in an outpatient clinic.
The exact incidence rate for isolated orchitis is not known but is rare.
Orchitis can lead to Infertility (male) infertility and testicular atrophy.
Isolated orchitis is rare and is usually concurrent with Epididymitis so the causative pathogens are similar.
In men younger than 35 years, STIs (STDs (gonococcal infections) Neisseria gonorrhoeae and STDs (chlamydia) Chlamydia trachomatis) are most frequently responsible for epididymitis.
Nonspecific bacterial Epididymitis is caused by various aerobic bacteria and is frequently associated with anatomic abnormalities.
In patients younger than 14 years and older than 35 years, epididymitis is generally from infection with common urinary pathogens such as Escherichia coli.
Among men who practice anal-insertive intercourse, E. Coli, other coliform bacteria, and Haemophilus influenzae are the common causative pathogens.
Other pathogens less commonly associated with epididymitis include Ureaplasma urealyticum, Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Mumps is the most frequent cause of viral orchitis and orchitis is the most common complication associated with mumps, occurring in 20% to 30% of males who contract mumps.
In patients with HIV/AIDS, mycobacteria, fungal and viral etiologies including Cytomegalovirus infection (adult and child)cytomegalovirus have been isolated.
In dairy farmers or cattle ranchers Brucella melitensis is another causative agent.
With the exception of viral diseases, genitourinary tract infections seldom involve the testes primarily. Blood-borne dissemination is the major route of isolated testicular infection.

Orchitis may be caused by number of different types of bacteria and viruses. It is usually a secondary result of epididymitis, inflammation of the tube that connects the vas deferens and the testicle.
Sexually active men should use condoms to prevent STIs. C

Sexually active men with acute infection should avoid sexual intercourse until they and their sex partners are cured (ie, until therapy is completed and patient and partners no longer have symptoms). C
Suspect orchitis in patients with a tender testicle, fever, and enlarged, tender inguinal lymph nodes. C
Consider epididymitis and testicular torsion in the differential diagnosis; they are much more common than orchitis. C
Mumps are a common cause in children. C

For men between the ages of 14 and 35 years, where STIs are the most common cause of epididymo-orchitis, obtain culture (urethra), nucleic hybridization tests (urethra), or nucleic acid amplification tests (urine) for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae. C
Patients often have unilateral pain that begins in the epididymis but can spread to the adjacent testicle.
Only 33% of patients complain of dysuria, while about 75% of patients complain of fever or chills.
Other symptoms include frequency, urgency, hematuria, and dysuria.
Viral orchitis is associated with abrupt onset of acute scrotal pain and swelling and is primarily unilateral.

On physical examination, the patient will have a tender swollen testis. There may be enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. The patient may have epididymal tenderness or prostate tenderness because of infection that spread to the testis.

Isolated testicular pain in the absence of symptoms or signs of infection should prompt the provider to look for testicular torsion. If torsion is in the differential diagnosis urgent referral to a urologist is needed.
CDC guidelines (2021) recommend examination of spun first void urine for white blood cells, leukocyte esterase test of urine, and if available Gram stain.

Obtain culture (urethra), nucleic hybridization tests (urethra), or nucleic acid amplification tests (urine) for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae in sexually active men. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) suggests that, due to higher sensitivity, nucleic acid amplification tests are preferred for the diagnosis of C. trachomatis.
Only one-third of patients have leukocytosis.
In patients with epididymo-orchitis, an elevated CRP is 96% sensitive and 94% specific.
About 40% of patients have pyuria and fewer than 20% have red blood cells in their urine. Urine culture is sterile about 75% of the time.
Ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality in distinguishing testicular torsion and orchitis.
Suspect orchitis in patients with unilateral pain in the scrotum accompanied by fever and lower abdominal pain.

Emergency testing and referral for testicular torsion is indicated when the onset of pain is sudden, pain is severe, or the initial examination do not support an accompanying diagnosis of Urethritis (male) urethritis or urinary-tract infection.
Obtain culture (urethra), nucleic hybridization tests (urethra), or nucleic acid amplification tests (urine) for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae in sexually active men.
In men younger than 14 years and older men, where enteric organisms are more likely causes, CDC guidelines (2021) recommend levofloxacin orally once daily for 10 days. C

For men where STIs are the most common cause of epididymo-orchitis, culture and treat empirically with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 10 days is recommended. C
For acute infection in men who practice insertive anal sex, cover both STIs and enteric organisms with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for 10 days. C
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics for pain, scrotal elevation, limitation of activity, and ice packs may be helpful. C
The value of interferon for mumps orchitis is unclear. B
Treating the cause of orchitis is effective in resolving the symptoms. Since most orchitis is caused by epididymitis, see that chapter for detailed treatment options.

In sexually active men, the CDC previously recommended fluoroquinolones. However, due to a rapid rise in resistant strains of N. gonorrhoeae, after obtaining diagnostic material CDC guidelines (2021) recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days when chlamydia or gonorrhea is the likely cause.

When the likely cause is either chlamydia, gonorrhea or enteric organisms (in men who practice insertive anal sex) ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose plus levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily for 10 days is recommended.
When enteric organisms are suspected as the likely cause (young children and older men without a history of anal insertive sex) then levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily is recommended for 10 days.

No controlled trials of interferon in men with mumps orchitis exist. In a single study where 4 men with bilateral mumps orchitis were treated with interferon, all acute symptoms disappeared within 4 days and after 6 to 15 months of follow-up, none developed testicular atrophy. In 2 very small studies of systemic alpha-2b interferon in children with mumps, 1 found fewer patients developed testicular atrophy while the other found no effect. Larger studies are needed.
Symptomatic relief with analgesics, elevation, bed rest and ice may be helpful but clinical trials are lacking.
Emergent referral to a urologist is warranted when testicular torsion is suspected.

Hospitalization is recommended for patients with intractable pain, pain suggests other diagnoses (such as torsion or abscess), inability to take oral medications, or Sepsis and septic shock (adult) sepsis.
Infertility may occur among patient with mumps orchitis, especially if bilateral, but good studies of the strength of association are lacking. C
Mumps is a common cause of orchitis in this age group.
Presents 3 to 10 days after parotitis in 20% to 30% of males.
